extracted.intended_audience: readers of 19th-century literary and political periodicals; educated general public interested in literature, society, and imperial policy
extracted.subtask_description: Short magazine/periodical essays and reviews covering literary criticism, social life (salon culture), and political/policy commentary typical of late-19th-century periodicals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate tone in correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Mrs. Montagu is at her best when addressing intimate friends: 'Her style is then easy and natural, and the good things that drop from her pen are worth picking up; but it is another affair when she writes to a stranger ... She then drags in gods and goddesses to adorn her pages, uses metaphor to straining, and moralises at wearisome length.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match style to audience: favour an easy, natural tone with intimate correspondents; avoid over-ornamentation, strained metaphor, and long moralising when writing to strangers or to 'dazzle' with learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic/dramatic merit depends on taste and skill, not rules
rubrics_metrics.description: "Rules can no more make a poet than receipts a cook. There must be taste, there must be skill." (in defence of Shakespeare against Voltaire's praise of strict classical unities)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value vigour, freedom, taste, and skill in drama and poetry over literal obedience to formal rules (e.g., Aristotle's unities). Formal correctness alone does not make great poetry or drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualities of a successful literary salon/hostess
rubrics_metrics.description: Mrs. Montagu 'collected around her the witty and the wise. Her salon quickly became the fashion.' Her gatherings discouraged cards; after-dinner company divided into animated conversational groups; she could 'hold her own in a brisk argument against four clever men.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful salon assembles intelligent, witty company; fosters animated conversation rather than card-playing; the hostess should be socially adept, hospitable (e.g., mid-day breakfasts), and intellectually engaged to keep discourse lively and respectable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superficial labeling of intellectual groups
rubrics_metrics.description: On 'Bluestocking' assemblies: 'A Bluestocking Club never existed. There was a Literary Club ... and to this the so-called bluestockings of both sexes belonged.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about derisive or reductive labels applied by outsiders; verify organizational facts before stereotyping a literary circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Landscape-gardening: adapt design to place and purse
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He adapts his scheme to the character of the place and my purse. We shall not erect temples to heathen gods, build proud bridges over humble rivulets, or do any of the marvellous things suggested by caprice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principles for landscape improvements: designs should harmonize with the site's character and the owner's budget; avoid capricious, overly grand or incongruous follies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Register-and-gradualist abolition method (Gordon's proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: General Gordon suggested the following as the effectual way of abolishing slavery: (1) The registration of all existing slaves. (2) Registers to be kept in each Government office of the names of slaves and their owners, with a description of each. (3) Every slave not registered within six months from a certain date to be free. (4) All slaves born after a certain date to be free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A procedural, administrative path to abolition: use registration and timed legal statuses rather than immediate blanket emancipation; Gordon proposed cancelling the existing Convention in favour of these measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat slave-hunting as murder and set phased legal deadlines
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Convention (Aug 4, 1877) it was agreed that slave-hunting should cease and that those engaged therein should be treated as murderers; trafficking between families would become illegal after specified dates (August 4, 1884 in lower Egypt; August 4, 1889 in the Soudan).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use international/colonial conventions to phase out the slave trade, set enforceable dates for criminalisation, and prepare the populace by promulgating a special ordinance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compensation vs confiscation principle in emancipation
rubrics_metrics.description: It would be 'as impolitic as it would be unjust' for a powerful nation to confiscate personal property (slaves) without compensation; Britain did not confiscate when emancipating its slaves—initially proposed a loan and ended with a gift (figures cited: loan of £15,000,000; gift of £20,000,000).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy for emancipation should consider legal/ethical claims of property and the political prudence of compensation or financial settlement rather than uncompensated confiscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority requirement for administrative/governmental acts
rubrics_metrics.description: General Gordon could not cancel the Convention or issue orders without deriving authority; 'How could he have issued any orders unless he derived his authority from the firman of the Khedive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure actions affecting legal/regulatory regimes are backed by proper commissions/firmans/mandates; individuals cannot unilaterally alter treaties or conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy feasibility and risk-assessment criteria for Sudan decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Critiques of proposals (evacuation, railway, relief routes) emphasise unanswered questions: where will the money come from for the railway; extreme hatred between Sudanese and Abyssinians; large numbers to be removed (40,000–50,000 persons for Khartoum and Sennaar alone); evacuation could take two years and entail great risk and bloodshed; abandonment might lead to barbarism and slave-raids.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate interventions by checking funding source, local inter-ethnic relations, logistics (population movements, timelines), and likely humanitarian/security consequences; do not recommend abandonment or large projects without these feasibility checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful interpretation of proclamations and reported statements
rubrics_metrics.description: On the puzzling proclamation of Feb 26 claiming Gordon had 'sent for British troops'—possible explanations include interpreter errors, misapprehension, or reference to other forces (Graham's force to Suakim) or to 200 Indian troops requested to Wadi-Halfa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing second-hand proclamations or translated statements, consider interpreter mistakes, ambiguous phrasing, and alternative referents before imputing falsehood or bad faith.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/political justification: strategic value and revenue considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument that Khartoum is 'as essential to Egypt as our frontier position at Quetta is to India' and that under Egyptian rule it returned a surplus revenue of over £100,000.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In territorial/political decisions, include strategic significance and fiscal impacts (revenue) in the evaluation; these factors weigh against simple abandonment.
